newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish insurers get support from savings market.
newsitem.headline: Swedish insurers get support from savings market.

text.p: Swedish insurers Trygg-Hansa and Skandia saw their margins squeezed in domestic non-life insurance in 1996, but that was not a disaster because the savings market was strong, analysts said on Wednesday.

"The development of Skandia's AFS is exciting and promises to be very good in 1997 and 1998," Nils Ringdal, analyst at Kleinwort Benson, said in reference to the Assurance & Financial Services savings operation.
"Quarter four last year showed more growth than earlier in the year, which indicates a strong momentum into 1997."

Skandia posted a one percent rise in operating profit to 2.39 billion crowns ($312.3 million) and a 12 percent return on net asset value after taxe compared with 14 percent in 1995. Pre-tax profit was 1.65 billion crowns against market expectations of 3.06 billion.
But analysts were taken by surprise by the company taking a 1.4 billion crown charge for a restructruing programme, which was expected to give long-term savings of 400 million crowns a year.
Ringdal was optimistic about the prospects for non-life premiums, saying: "Non-life insurance premiums could rise in 1998 again as premium prices move in waves up and down internationally."
But Jesper Skriver Frandsen, analyst at Aros Securities, was more cautious regarding non-life insurance, saying the long term trend showed much tougher competition.
Skandia's technical result for its Nordic non-life insurance and reinsurance operations more than halved to 426 million crowns ($55.7 million) in 1996 from 1.10 billion crowns a year earlier.
"The decline is attributable to a weak first half year with high claim costs in Denmark and Sweden," the company said in its 1996 earnings report released on Wednesday.
But Ringdal was not too worried by the figures.
"The negative non-life insurance development in Sweden, Denmark and Britain does not mean a risk for the share price as AFS will give strong positive effects," he said.
Trygg-Hansa last month posted a 8.8 percent fall in total 1996 preliminary non-life insurance premiums to 5.90 billion crowns.
It did not break the figure down by market, but said there was a "stable result trend for Swedish non-life insurance despite lower premium volume."
Both groups showed growth in their savings operations with Skandia saying premiums written by its life and unit linked assurance operations rose 36 percent to 36.42 billion crowns.
"The positive growth in Skandia's total premiums exceeds expectations due to the unit linked performance," Frandsen said.
Skandia's total premiums rose 16 percent to 58.79 billion crowns last year.
Trygg-Hansa said the premiums of its unit linked operations rose 42 percent to 920 million crowns, while premiums written by Trygg-Hansa Life rose 13 percent to 5.29 billion crowns.
Analysts did not want to say much about Trygg-Hansa's preliminary earnings as they were waiting for the company's complete and final 1996 report, due on March 20.

Regarding Skandia, analysts welcomed a proposal to increase the dividend to 2.75 crowns a share from two as well as the company adopting a new dividend policy corresponding to 15 to 25 percent of operating profit after tax.
Skandia's share fell three crowns to close at 225 crowns, while Trygg-Hansa's share dropped 4.5 crowns to 150 crowns.
-- Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1006 ($ = 7.653 Swedish Crowns)
